newsitem.title: USA: Cystic fibrosis gene test should be offered: panel.
newsitem.headline: Cystic fibrosis gene test should be offered: panel.

text.p: A U.S. advisory panel on Wednesday urged doctors to offer cystic fibrosis tests to everyone considering having a baby.

In the broadest recommendation since genetic testing began, the panel strongly emphasized that the test would not be mandatory, it must be confidential, and must be accompanied by appropriate education and genetic counseling. Insurers, they said, should pay for it.

Doctors should be neutral and not push potential parents into either having or shunning the test. But they should make couples aware that the test is available, the panel of outside experts, convened for a "consensus development conference" by the National Institutes of Health, concluded.
"The word 'offered' was very carefully considered," said panel member Dr. James Evans, who practices in Durham, N.C.

It was the first time a panel such as this has backed population-wide testing for a genetic disease. Other genetic tests are recommended for people known to be at high risk for a specific inherited disease such as Tay-Sachs.

"As more and more genetic tests for a variety of diseases become available, it is important for both health care providers and patients to understand the limitations and implications of such tests," said panel chairman Dr. Rodney Howell of the University of Miami.
"Our recommendations for cystic fibrosis testing may serve as a guide for the complex testing issues that will undoubtedly arise with other inherited diseases," he added.

About 25,000 Americans have cystic fibrosis and about 850 children are diagnosed each year. Although treatments have improved the quality and length of their lives since the 1970s, most still die by their early 30s.

The panelists took pains to point out that they were not encouraging people to abort fetuses that will develop the disease, or denigrating the lives of people who do have cystic fibrosis, which affects the lungs and pancreas.
But they said the test can help parents make informed reproductive choices.

"Some participants in studies have sought information in anticipation of a decision about pregnancy termination in the case of a fetus with CF. Others wished only to know their carrier status, perhaps to make emotional and practical plans for parenting a child with CF," the panel said.
They did not recommend screening of all newborns as there is no therapeutic value as of now.

If only one parent has a defective CF gene, he or she is a carrier and the child will not have the disease. If both parents have a defect, there is a one-in-four chance that a pregnancy will produce a child with the incurable disorder.
The gene was discovered in 1989. The test is already commercially available, and costs $50 to $150. Counseling costs are extra.

A few years ago, experts opposed widespread testing, partly because of all the ethical problems raised by gene tests and partly because tests were not good enough to detect the 600-odd mutations that can cause CF.
Although the test is still not perfect, it is nearing the 90 percent sensitivity threshold, with higher rates for some ethnic groups. The panelists consider that level acceptable.
CF is more common among whites of Northern European descent and Ashkenazi Jews (of East European origin) than among blacks and Asians.
Studies on groups offered the tests show that about half and maybe as many as three-quarters opt to have the screening, although those figures may not mirror trends in the overall U.S. population.
